papers.title: Reaching the intrinsic performance limits of superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors up to 0.1 mm wide
papers.abstract: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) combine high detection efficiency, low noise, and excellent timing resolution, making them a leading platform for photon-counting applications. However, despite decades of materials and fabrication research, detector performance has never been shown to match theoretical performance expectations. Here, we demonstrate for the first time in situ tuning of a detector from its typical, suboptimal operation, to a regime limited only by material quality, allowing the device to reach its intrinsic performance limit. Our approach is based on current-biased superconducting "rails" placed on either side of the detector that redistribute current across its width to achieve its peak performance. This technique reduces the dark count rate by ten orders of magnitude. Further, we show operation at this intrinsic performance limit for devices up to 0.1 mm wide, and also demonstrate near-unity internal detection efficiency (IDE) at a wavelength of 4um for a 20um-wide detector--a factor of 20 wider than the current state of the art. This work enables future detectors to overcome the Pearl limit for device width, paving the way for arbitrarily large detectors.

summary.summary: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) with widths up to 100 µm are tuned to their intrinsic performance limit using adjacent current-biased superconducting rails that redistribute current density across the wire width, achieving a ten orders-of-magnitude reduction in dark count rates and near-unity internal detection efficiency at 4 µm for 20 µm-wide detectors. This rail-based current redistribution suppresses edge vortex penetration, enabling operation limited only by vortex-antivortex pair unbinding in the bulk and overcoming the Pearl length ($\Lambda \approx 600$ µm) limitation on device width.
summary.motivation: SNSPDs achieve high detection efficiency and low jitter but operate well below the depairing current $I_d$ due to current crowding at wire edges, which creates a fundamental barrier to scaling beyond the Pearl length and limits infrared sensitivity in wide devices.
summary.method: The authors placed 4 µm-wide Nb rails (50 nm thick) adjacent to 3 nm-thick WSi SNSPD wires and varied the rail current $I_r$ to invert the current density profile $J(x)$, using London equation calculations and thermal transport measurements at 900 mK to characterize dark counts, photon detection, and timing jitter.
summary.result: For a 50 µm-wide device, $I_r = I_r^* \approx 11.8$ mA increased the switching current ratio $I_{\mathrm{sw}}/I_d$ and extended the detection plateau at 1550 nm by 40%; for a 100 µm-wide device, more than 10 orders of magnitude dark count reduction and 44% plateau widening were achieved; near-unity internal detection efficiency was demonstrated at 4 µm for a 20 µm-wide detector (factor of 20 wider than prior state-of-the-art), with timing jitter improved by ~30%.
